newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan foreign minister to visit India.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan foreign minister to visit India.

text.p: Pakistan's caretaker foreign minister hopes to meet his Indian counterpart during this month's ministerial meeting of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), his spokesman said on Thursday.

But the spokesman said that Foreign Minister Sahibzada Yaqoob Khan was not expected to have any formal talks with Indian Foreign Minister I.K. Gujral during the two-day SAARC meeting that starts in New Delhi on December 19.

"There are going to be bilateral meetings among leaders of the delegations that will involve meetings between leaders of the Pakistan and Indian delegations," he said. "But it does not mean there will be any formal bilateral discussion."
"Our foreign minister will take advantage of his stay in New Delhi to have useful discussions with various leaders of public opinion in India. There will be no formal bilateral dialogue."
The spokesman said Pakistan wanted good neighbourly relations with India to promote regional peace and stability.
"It was Pakistan which earlier this year renewed an offer of talks, but certain actions by India vitiated the atmosphere."
He was referring to state assembly elections held in Indian-controlled Jammu and Kashmir in September for the first time in six years. Islamabad denounced the polls as a sham.
"The so-called political process in (Indian-held Kashmir) has no relevance to the central issue, which is the exercise of the right of self-determination by Kashmiris," he said.
India and Pakistan broke off high-level talks in January 1994 when New Delhi baulked at Islamabad's insistence that the main focus be on the disputed Himalayan region of Kashmir.
The two countries have fought three wars since their independence from Britain in 1947, two of them over Kashmir.
Tension has run high since the start in 1990 of a separatist revolt by Moslem guerrillas that has cost an estimated 20,000 lives in the two-thirds of Kashmir ruled by New Delhi.
Islamabad, which controls the remaining third of Kashmir, denies Indian charges that it is training and arming the militants, who seek independence or union with Pakistan.
